data.title: Middle East Eye: What missiles and drones do the Houthis have?
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
What missiles and drones do the Houthis have?
A rapid offensive by Yemen’s Houthis has intensified the country’s civil war and caused chaos in global oil markets.
The group, which has controlled much of northern Yemen for over a decade, has seized fresh territory from the pro-government forces and threatened shipping traffic, notably that of Saudi Arabia, in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the maritime chokepoint linking the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
With few signs of military formality, the group has often been described in international media as a "ragtag fighting force".
But over the past two decades, the Houthis have evolved to use missiles and drones to stage attacks inside Yemen as well as against Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, among others.
Much of the group’s arsenal has either been designed or supplied by Iran, which regards the force as a member of its Axis of Resistance, a network of allies that also includes Hamas and Hezbollah.
The Houthis have also acquired weapons, including decades-old Soviet-era tanks and helicopters, after victory on the battlefield, and recently seized US-supplied military vehicles captured from retreating Saudi-backed forces.
While the Houthis’ stockpile levels are unknown, it is possible to assemble a sense of their firepower and military capabilities.

Israeli forces killed at least eight Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Wednesday as ceasefire violations continued a year after the agreement was signed.
An Israeli air strike hit a civilian transport vehicle in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood of western Gaza City, killing five people and wounding 15 others, including women and children.
The strike hit a cart attached to a minibus used to transport passengers amid severe fuel shortages and soaring transport costs across the enclave.
Such vehicles are often packed with dozens of people travelling between different areas of the Strip.
“The Israeli missile struck the civilian transport vehicle at a crowded hour of the day, when the streets were full of displaced people moving around,” Motaz Ayoub, a civil defence ambulance officer who was among the first responders to reach the scene, told Middle East Eye.
“When we arrived, many of the killed and wounded were scattered across the street. We did not know who they were or where they had come from. One man's body was cut off, and many of the injured were in critical condition.”
Ayoub said a bus passing close to the vehicle was also hit, leaving several passengers wounded.

He is being abandoned even by his closest allies.
It was perhaps not surprising that 77 nations, including a handful of European states, walked out of the chamber in protest that a wanted war crimes suspect - a fugitive from the International Criminal Court (ICC) - was being given a platform to speak on the world’s largest stage.
Far more notable was what happened - or rather, didn’t - away from the podium. Netanyahu spent just eight hours in the US before heading back to Israel. It is hard to believe that that was his choice.
He was denied his usual moment in the sun with Donald Trump at the White House, and could not even secure a meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
There was no invitation to address the US Congress, and with it familiar scenes of legislators rapturously celebrating his anti-Palestinian incitement.
Israel's former ambassador to Washington, Michael Oren, told Reuters: "I don't recall a time when the prime minister came to the United States and didn't meet with the president.”
The shunning of Netanyahu stood in stark contrast to the reception of Xi Jinping. The Chinese leader was personally greeted at the airport by Trump with a red carpet and military flyover.

Each episode will feature conversations with Palestinians about what life is like in the strip, from displacement and destruction to shortages of food, water and medical care, as well as the struggles to maintain family life.
The first episode will feature an extended conversation with Mariam Yusuf, a recent medical graduate who shares what it was like to seek refuge in a hospital during Israel’s bloody war on Gaza.
She recounts being forced into quarantine after contracting chickenpox, losing loved ones to starvation, and the struggle to process her grief amid the devastation around her.
"The genocide in Gaza has been normalised. What happens there is now openly being used as a model to try elsewhere, in the occupied West Bank and Lebanon," said David Hearst, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of MEE.
"Gaza has been reduced to numbers. This podcast gives Palestinians the space to tell their own stories and relate their own experiences.

data.author: Wladimir van Wilgenburg
data.summary:
‘We are vulnerable’: Kurds fear renewed attacks as US‑led coalition departs Iraq
Submitted by
Wladimir van Wilgenburg
on
Thu, 10/01/2026 - 11:02
As Washington ends its decade‑long mission in Iraq, Kurds warn autonomous region is at risk amid US-Iran tensions
Kurdish Peshmerga fighters about 60km south of Erbil, capital of Iraq's autonomous Kurdish region, on 30 September 2026 (Safin Hamid/AFP)
Off
On 28 September, residents of Erbil heard military aircraft overhead as the US‑led coalition against the Islamic State group (IS) was preparing for its full withdrawal.
That same night, three Iranian drones hit a camp belonging to an Iranian Kurdish opposition party in Koya. Two days later, Koya was hit again by a drone, the first such attack after the coalition’s departure.
On Wednesday, the US‑led coalition ended its more than decade‑long mission in Iraq, a mission that began in 2014 when IS seized large territories in Iraq and Syria and carried out mass atrocities.
Although the militant group was declared defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, coalition forces remained to help contain its remnants.
In 2024, Baghdad and Washington agreed to wind down the mission, prompting a gradual withdrawal from bases across Iraq and a final consolidation in the Kurdistan Region before the complete pullout, scheduled for 30 September.
The latest incidents in Koya underscore how exposed the Iraqi Kurdistan Region remains to drone and missile attacks amid ongoing tensions between Iran and the United States.
According to a 27 September statement from the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs – the military forces of the autonomous Kurdish region – Iraqi Kurdistan has endured more than a thousand drone and ballistic missile attacks since Israel and the US launched the war on Iran on 28 February, causing casualties and significant material damage.

data.title: Middle East Eye: South Lebanon: 'It’s torture, they are razing our lives before our eyes'
data.author: Laurent Perpigna Iban
data.summary:
South Lebanon: 'It’s torture, they are razing our lives before our eyes'
Submitted by
Laurent Perpigna Iban
on
Wed, 09/30/2026 - 11:10
Residents of the village of Mansouri are watching helplessly as the Israeli military methodically destroys their town
Standing on a hill in the Hanniyeh village in south Lebanon, people from neighbouring Mansouri watch as Israeli occupation forces raze their village (Laurent Iban Perpigna/MEE)
Off
Day after day, the Israeli-occupied village of Mansouri, perched on a green hill a few kilometres south of the coastal city of Tyre, is slowly disappearing. Already heavily damaged during the war, it is now quite literally being wiped off the map, in a final twist of cynicism, during the ceasefire.
The Israeli army, which has made it one of its main theatres of operations for weeks, is sparing no effort: demolitions with explosives and air strikes have followed one another at a relentless pace in recent days, to the despair of the village’s roughly 5,000 inhabitants.
The village, which the Israeli army presents as an operational stronghold of Hezbollah, was initially located outside the “Yellow Line”, the “security” demarcation imposed by Israel on Lebanese territory shortly after the latest ceasefire came into effect.
Even then, residents Middle East Eye spoke to following the ceasefire feared that the zone would eventually swallow up their village. It now has, although officially only in part: the Yellow Line cuts through Mansouri, dividing it in two.
On paper, that is, as the village is now entirely occupied – this summer, all the residents who had returned to the area had no choice but to flee once again, under fire from the Israeli air force, which continues its operations.
The village mayor has denounced in the local press “attacks against residents using artillery, as well as hand grenades and stun grenades dropped by drones”. He himself miraculously survived after being wounded in an Israeli attack.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli attacks kill Palestinian and wound others north of Khan Younis
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Israeli attacks kill Palestinian and wound others north of Khan Younis
Israeli attacks on Wednesday evening killed a Palestinian and wounded several others in the north of Khan Younis, Wafa news agency reports.
According to the report, the attack targeted people on the Salah Ad-Din Street, killing a 33-year-old and wounding others, including a minor.
This comes amid a wave of Israeli attacks on Wednesday, which killed at least eight people. MEE reported earlier that an Israeli strike hit a civilian transport vehicle in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood of western Gaza City, killing five people and wounding 15 others, including women and children.
Meanwhile, Gaza's government media office reported that Palestinian journalist Muhammad Abdel Aziz al-Najjar was killed in a separate attack on Wednesday. The office did not provide any further details relating to the attack, but stated that he was the 263rd journalist killed by Israel since October 2023.
Israeli forces have killed at least 1,430 people since the ceasefire was signed, an average of around four people a day.
They include at least 300 children.
The agreement was intended to end Israel’s genocide and lift restrictions on the entry of aid and commercial goods.
Israel has repeatedly violated the agreement, carrying out near-daily bombing raids while maintaining tight restrictions on the entry of aid and goods.
Overall, Israeli forces have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since the genocide began in October 2023 and wounded more than 175,000 others.
